content.text:
Dallas ISD (057905) — the four money questions Texas reports separately.
1. OUTSIDE the operating total: $3,578 per student a year in debt service, higher than 83% of Texas districts (state median $1,538).
2. WHO PAYS: 79c of every revenue dollar is raised locally against 54c statewide, on gross collections.
3. THE BALLOT: $14.3B approved by voters across 15 propositions since 2002; 1% of what was asked named athletics — an UPPER BOUND, because propositions bundle purposes.
4. WHERE IT LANDED: 42.0% at Meets against 36.5% predicted by this district's own student need (+5.5 points).

What stands out:
  - Debt costs more than half of what instruction costs: 50¢ goes to debt for every dollar that reaches a classroom. None of it appears in the operating total TEA reports.
  - Sends money back to the state: $376 per student leaves under recapture — $52,538,602 a year. TEA reports this district's revenue after that is taken out.
  - Paid for locally, not by the state: 79% of revenue is raised from local property, against 54% statewide.
  - Does better than its student need predicts: 42.0% at Meets against 36.5% predicted — +5.5 points.

These are descriptions of published numbers against published thresholds, not findings of wrongdoing, and there is deliberately no combined score.

  Share of the operating dollar reaching a classroom: 60.0% -> 50.7% — moving that way faster than Texas as a whole
  Instruction per student: $8,240 -> $7,018 — moving that way faster than Texas as a whole
  Debt service per student: $1,131 -> $3,485 — moving that way faster than Texas as a whole

A trend is a direction, not a cause: a falling instruction share can be a district cutting classrooms or opening them, and this data cannot tell the two apart.

limits: A trend describes a direction, not a cause. A falling instruction share can be a district cutting classrooms or a district opening them; this data cannot tell the two apart.
Operating balance compares operating revenue with operating spending only. Including debt service or capital would count buildings paid for out of bond proceeds as a deficit.

The shift between functions is real reallocation, not reclassification: the 16 function codes still sum to the reported operating total in every year, risers and fallers cancel to a zero residual, no single function absorbs the decline, and it predates COVID and continues after the federal money left. Dallas ISD (057905) put 15 bond propositions to voters between 2002 and 2026; 12 carried (80.0%). Asked $14,442,670,000, approved $14,289,770,000.
Most recent:
  2020-11-03  $33.5M  defeated  Natatorium
  2026-05-02  $5.9B  carried  School Building & Buses
  2026-05-02  $144.7M  carried  Technology
  2026-05-02  $143.3M  carried  Maintenance
  2026-05-02  $26.2M  carried  Swimming Pool

The ballot is the only public record of what school debt was FOR — TEA does not itemise facilities. Amounts are as asked, in the dollars of their own year, and are not inflation-adjusted.

limits: Propositions bundle purposes. A proposition reading 'School Building & Gymnasium' is counted under athletics, so athletics dollars are an upper bound; the athletics-only figure is reported separately.
Amounts are as asked, in the dollars of their year, and are not inflation-adjusted — counts and pass rates are the comparable measures across eras.
Purpose is free text written by hundreds of districts over 66 years; the keyword rules used to classify it are published above.

About a fifth of records carry a vote tally under 20 (a multi-million-dollar bond recorded as '1 for, 0 against'). Those are placeholders rather than turnout, so the tally is shown as unreported. The carried/defeated result itself is unaffected.

content.text:
Dallas ISD (057905) still owes $7.2B as of fiscal 2025: $4.6B of principal and $2.6B of interest not yet paid (36.4% of the total).
That is $51,861 per student, owed over decades rather than in a year. On debt already sold it clears in 2054.
Borrowing to build schools is lawful and ordinary, and this is a balance sheet rather than a budget — it sits outside TEA's operating total entirely and is not comparable to it.

limits: Figures are as of fiscal 2025, the Board's most recent completed year. Years after it are the amortisation schedule for debt already sold, not a forecast of future borrowing — districts will issue more, so the schedule is a floor.
Excludes obligations maturing in under a year, commercial paper, and special obligations that do not require Attorney General approval, per the Board's own scope note.

Dollars repaid per dollar borrowed is reported at each district's PEAK year, not the current one. On outstanding balances the ratio rises on its own as principal is retired and is not a measure of anything.

No ratio is reported where CAB principal never reached $5m in any year on record. Below that the figure is dominated by a nearly-retired balance, and for districts whose bonds were sold before 2005, or whose reported years have a gap, the record never shows the deal at all. Their deferred interest is still reported — it is the ratio, not the debt, that is unknowable here.
Debt outstanding is not comparable to a district's operating budget: it is a stock owed over decades, and it sits outside TEA's operating total entirely.
68 of the Board's 1,035 listed school districts publish no series and carry no Board-tracked debt.

content.text:
Dallas ISD (057905) spent $15,160 per student in Census current spending, fiscal 2024.
That is more per student than 43% of the 9,294 U.S. districts with 500+ students (the middle one spends $15,770).
Texas as a whole ranks 44 of 51 (50 states and the District of Columbia; territories excluded) at $13,642 per student in average daily attendance, NPEFS fiscal 2024. Dividing by fall membership instead moves Texas only to 45, so the denominator choice is not the story.
Current spending is the Census's own figure and EXCLUDES construction, land and debt — it is smaller than, and never mixed with, the TEA all-funds figures other tools here report. Fiscal 2024 is an earlier year than the TEA data on this site; never blend the two in one number.

texas.who: 50 states and the District of Columbia; territories excluded

national.pool_rule: U.S. districts with 500+ students and a positive per-pupil current spending figure

limits: Census fiscal 2024 — one year behind the TEA fiscal 2025 figures elsewhere on this site. The two are never mixed in one figure.

Current spending only: the Census excludes construction, land, debt, and spending for students outside a district's fall membership, so this figure runs below the all-in per-student total shown elsewhere on this site.
The state ranking divides by average daily attendance, NCES's own denominator; dividing by fall membership instead moves Texas only from 44 to 45 of 51.

Texas charter schools have no Census F-33 row at all — the Census surveys governments, and charters are not independent governments — so they have no national percentile, by construction rather than by omission.
Districts under 500 students are shown but not ranked, the same rule used across this site.

content.text:
Texas school finance, 1,202 districts.
Debt service OUTSIDE TEA's operating total: $13.9B a year, median $1,538 per student.
Who pays: 54c local, 37c state, 9c federal, on gross collections. 224 districts pay recapture.
Ballot record: 4,992 propositions since 1958, $327.6B asked, $262.0B approved.

Seventeen years (fiscal 2009-2025, constant 2024 dollars):
  The classroom's share of the operating dollar has fallen for seventeen years: 57.8% → 54.5%
  Debt service is where the money went: $1,507 → $2,441 per student
  Security spending has more than doubled: $96 → $232 per student
  The federal money that masked it has gone: $2,798 (2022) → $1,432
  For the first time in seventeen years, Texas districts together spent more on operations than operating revenue brought in: +$3.0B (2022) → −$1.6B (2025)
  The growth that used to pay for it has stopped: 12,807 students a year, was 68,869

Did passing a bond change results? +1.31 points, CI +0.07 to +2.55, p=0.038 — SUGGESTIVE, NOT SETTLED. It crossed the conventional line only when a district-matching bug was fixed. Do not report it as proof that bonds raise test scores.

did_it_work.window: results 2-4 years after the vote against the 3 years before, each district compared with itself
did_it_work.caveat: A bond in a growing district buys seats, not scores, and safety and roofs are real goods a test cannot see. This measures test results only.

trend_findings.headline: The classroom's share of the operating dollar has fallen for seventeen years
trend_findings.detail: Instruction took 57.8% of every operating dollar in 2009 and 54.5% in 2025, a fall of 3.3 points. In constant dollars that is $369 less per student on teaching, while total spending per student rose. Re-derived on only the 1,142 districts reporting in both years, the fall is 3.2 points — so this is not a change in who reports.

trend_findings.headline: Debt service is where the money went
trend_findings.detail: Up 62% in constant dollars since 2009. None of it appears in TEA's operating total, so a district can look lean on instruction while carrying the state's heaviest debt.

trend_findings.headline: Security spending has more than doubled
trend_findings.detail: A 2.4-fold rise in constant dollars — the largest proportional increase of any function, and it comes out of the same operating dollar as instruction.

trend_findings.headline: The federal money that masked it has gone
trend_findings.detail: Federal revenue per student peaked in 2022 and is down 49% since, in constant dollars — back below where it started in 2009.

trend_findings.headline: For the first time in seventeen years, Texas districts together spent more on operations than operating revenue brought in
trend_findings.detail: 534 of 1,202 districts (44.4%) spent more on operations than operating revenue covered in 2025, and they enrol 67.7% of Texas students. The worst any earlier year in this window reached was 27.1%. Operating revenue against operating spending only: debt service and construction are excluded on both sides, and so is the debt tax levy that pays for them — otherwise a routine building year reads as a crisis.

trend_findings.headline: The growth that used to pay for it has stopped
trend_findings.detail: Texas districts added about 68,869 students a year through the 2010s. Over the last two years they added 25,614 in total. Debt service and fixed costs do not shrink when growth does.
